analysis.one_liner: Expands the tax credit employers can claim for providing child care to workers.
analysis.headline: The House referred the bill to the Ways and Means Committee in May 2025, and it has received no further action in the 119th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill roughly triples the tax credit employers get for building or supporting child care for their workers, raising the credit rate from 25% to 40% (50% for small businesses, 60% in rural or low-income areas) and lifting the annual dollar cap about eightfold. It also requires Treasury to publicize the credit and directs a government study on child care regulations. The bill has not moved since its referral to committee in May 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that sponsor child care for employees receive a much larger tax credit, worth up to $1.2 million a year per employer. Workers at firms that choose to build or fund child care would gain access to on-site or subsidized care. Small businesses and firms in rural or low-income areas get the highest credit rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers sponsoring child care for workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the employer-provided child care credit rate from 25% to 40% of qualified expenses, 50% for businesses with 500 or fewer employees, and 60% for facilities in low-income census tracts or rural counties [S2].
It lifts the annual cap on qualified expenses to $2 million and the maximum annual credit to $1.2 million, up from the $150,000 cap under current law [S2].
It directs the Treasury Department to run a public awareness program so eligible employers know the credit exists and how to claim it [S2].
It directs the Government Accountability Office to study state licensing rules and report on reducing barriers for multi-employer and multi-state child care facilities [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $1.2 million a year in forgiven tax revenue per claiming employer. Families whose employers do not participate receive nothing directly; the benefit reaches parents only through their employer's decision to opt in.

drawbacks.text: The benefit reaches children and parents only indirectly: an employer must choose to spend money on child care before the credit does anything, so workers at firms that do not participate — disproportionately lower-wage workers — get no help [S2].

The higher caps primarily advantage larger firms that can afford to build facilities; child care is steered through employers rather than provided to families directly, adding the workplace to the list of benefits Americans depend on their employer for [S2].

The bill costs the Treasury revenue with no cap on total national cost, and its study directing a report on reducing regulatory 'burdens' on child care providers could feed efforts to loosen licensing and safety rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill could meaningfully expand employer-sponsored child care, especially at small businesses and in rural areas where the credit rate is highest, and simply telling employers the credit exists addresses the fact that it has been little used. But the design helps only families whose employers opt in, gives the largest tax breaks to firms already positioned to build facilities, and costs revenue that could instead fund child care aid families could take anywhere. It is a modest, employer-centered approach to a problem that broader policy could address more directly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on May 1, 2025, and the committee has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Rep. David Kustoff (R-TN) introduced the bill on May 1, 2025, joined by Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-NY), and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S2][S4].
No markup, hearing, or floor vote has occurred, and no additional cosponsors have joined [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet: the bill sits in committee. Employers who would claim the larger credit and parents waiting on employer child care both wait; the current law remains unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits untouched in committee

for.name: Rep. David Kustoff
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand the employer-provided child care credit.

for.name: Rep. Claudia Tenney
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Republicans and no Democrats have signed on, but no one has actively opposed the bill — it simply has not moved.

industries.note: Employers can claim up to $1.2 million a year in tax credits for sponsoring child care. Workers only benefit if their employer chooses to participate, so the industry gains a tax break while the public gain is conditional.

Employer demand for on-site and contracted child care would grow, benefiting providers. But the bill's study directs federal attention to reducing state licensing and regulatory requirements, which providers have long sought and safety advocates caution against.
Businesses with 500 or fewer employees get a 50% credit rate, higher than the general 40%, making it easier for them to offer child care to lower-wage workers.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with a single sponsor and cosponsor that sit in Ways and Means without a hearing almost never reach the floor on their own. The realistic path would be absorption into a larger tax package; absent that, it is likely to expire at the end of this Congress.
